top_choice_rationale: On the common criteria, Cărtărescu (P001) has the most defensible case: a voice recognizable at the level of the sentence, formal control of very large structures, and imaginative depth in which memory, the body and dream carry metaphysical questions. This is publicly described in Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid. My answer on development versus elaboration is provisional. Public description suggests Solenoid changes frame and register, but I cannot show this textually and have read no source independently. The citation should name the prose architecture and credit the poetry at most as origin. If colleagues who read Romanian show that the later novels only restate the trilogy, the wording should be narrowed to the works where control is demonstrable. Adonis (P002) is a serious second choice. Remaking the poetic language of a whole tradition may be a greater achievement, and the committee is poorly placed to test its prosodic core through translation. I rank him above no award because a narrowly worded poetry-only citation can be written. I rank him below P001 because the Cărtărescu claim can be partly verified through translation, and that matters for what a citation can responsibly claim. It is not a finding that his achievement is smaller. P000 is last because the uncertainties bear on the wording of the citation, not on whether a citation can be stated.
recusal_note: None apparent from the profile, which records no personal or institutional tie to Cărtărescu or Adonis. As disclosure only, not a recusal ground: my scholarship on the fragment, modern poetry and exile literature, and my Celan translation, overlap thematically with the poetics attributed to Adonis, which is relevant to how my second-ranked choice should be scrutinized. I cannot rule out that this background affects my ordering. The profile documents no committee votes or preferences, and none are claimed.
